intro: AI systems have an attack surface that older security checklists miss. This module maps that surface from data collection to end users, shows how to adapt STRIDE and data flow diagrams for machine learning applications, and introduces the two reference taxonomies defenders use to share findings: MITRE ATLAS and the NIST adversarial machine learning taxonomy in AI 100-2. You finish by rating threats by attacker access, impact and likelihood so mitigations can be prioritized.

lessons.title: The AI attack surface
lessons.why: You cannot defend what you have not listed, and an AI system has more entry points than a conventional application.

p: A conventional application has code, a database and an API. An AI system adds a data supply chain, a training process, model artifacts and a probabilistic component whose behavior depends on inputs in ways no one fully specified. The attack surface is every place an adversary can read, write or influence something that shapes model behavior or consumes model output. Listing these places is the first step of any assessment.
A useful way to list them is to follow the life cycle: data, training, artifact, deployment, inference, and the surrounding application.

Data collection and labeling accept input from scrapers, partners, users and annotators; any of them can inject poisoned samples or biased labels. The training environment holds compute, notebooks, credentials and datasets, and attacks there include stolen credentials, malicious dependencies and tampered jobs. Model artifacts such as weights, checkpoints and adapters are files that can be stolen, swapped or trojaned, and formats like Python pickle can execute code when loaded.
Registries and hubs, internal or public, are the distribution channel for those artifacts and need integrity checks.

At serving, the inference API accepts adversarial inputs, prompts and high-volume query sequences used for model extraction or membership inference. Output channels matter too: model text rendered in a browser or passed to a shell can become cross-site scripting or command injection. Plugins, tools and connectors extend the model's reach to email, files and databases, so a manipulated model becomes a privileged actor.
Users are part of the surface: they paste secrets into prompts, trust fabricated answers and can be targeted by AI-generated social engineering.

Do not forget ordinary infrastructure. GPU clusters, object storage buckets holding datasets, CI/CD runners that build model images, observability tools that log prompts, and vector databases that store embeddings all carry classic vulnerabilities such as exposed endpoints, weak IAM and unpatched software. Many real incidents in AI platforms were conventional misconfigurations, such as an open notebook server or a public bucket, rather than exotic attacks on models. Assess both layers together: the classical controls protect the foundations that the AI-specific controls assume.

lessons.example: A team builds a support chatbot on a hosted model with a RAG index of help pages and a tool that opens tickets. Their inventory lists: public wiki as a data source (poisoning), vector database (cross-tenant retrieval), chat API (injection, cost abuse), the ticket tool (excessive agency), logs containing chat text (privacy), and the vendor API key in the CI system (secret theft). Each item gets an owner and a control.

lessons.title: Threat modeling AI systems
lessons.why: A structured model turns a vague worry about AI risk into a list of specific threats with owners and controls.

sections.h: Start with a data flow diagram
p: Threat modeling begins with a data flow diagram (DFD). Draw external entities such as users and partners, processes such as the chat service and the training job, data stores such as the vector database and dataset bucket, and the flows between them. Then draw trust boundaries where data crosses between zones of different privilege: internet to API gateway, application to model provider, application to tools, data lake to training cluster.
Threats cluster at boundaries and on flows that cross them, so each crossing gets scrutiny.

STRIDE gives six threat categories: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service and Elevation of privilege. Applied to ML, tampering includes data poisoning, backdoored weights and prompt injection that alters behavior. Information disclosure includes model extraction, membership inference, training data leakage and system prompt leakage. Denial of service includes resource exhaustion and denial of wallet. Elevation of privilege includes an injected agent using tools beyond the user's rights.
Spoofing covers stolen API keys and impersonated data sources; repudiation covers missing logs of who changed a dataset.

Extend the standard questions with AI-specific ones. Who can write to training or retrieval data? Can an attacker see model outputs, scores or logits? Are weights stored in a format that can run code? What happens if the model is confidently wrong or manipulated? Which tool actions can it trigger? What data enters prompts and where do prompts get logged?
Frameworks such as the OWASP LLM Top 10, MITRE ATLAS and NIST AI RMF supply checklists you can map threats onto, which improves coverage and gives stakeholders familiar vocabulary.

For each threat record the affected asset, the entry point, the attacker, the potential impact, existing controls and the planned mitigation. Prioritize with likelihood and impact, assign an owner and a due date, and decide how you will test that the control works. Revisit the model when the architecture changes, for example when a new tool is added or a new data source is connected, because these are exactly the moments when the attack surface grows. A threat model that sits in a slide deck and is never updated provides little protection.

snippet.label: Threat table excerpt
snippet.text:
ID  Flow                  STRIDE  Threat                          Control
T1  user -> chat API      T/E     Prompt injection hijacks tools  Tool allow-list, approval
T2  wiki -> vector DB     T       Poisoned article retrieved      Source vetting, signing
T3  chat API -> logs      I       PII stored in prompts           Redaction, retention limit
T4  client -> chat API    D       Token flood, cost spike         Rate limit, quotas

lessons.example: For the chatbot at example.com the DFD shows a boundary between the internet and the API gateway, another between the app and the hosted model provider, and a third between the app and the ticketing system. Applying STRIDE at the third boundary yields elevation of privilege: an injected prompt could cause ticket creation or modification with the bot's service account. The mitigation is a scoped token that can only create tickets in one queue.

lessons.title: MITRE ATLAS tactics and techniques
lessons.why: ATLAS gives defenders a shared language and a structured way to describe how attacks against AI unfold.

p: MITRE ATLAS (Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems) is a knowledge base of adversary tactics, techniques and real-world case studies for AI systems, modeled on MITRE ATT&CK. Tactics describe the attacker's goal at a stage, such as Reconnaissance or Exfiltration. Techniques describe how, and each has an ID with the prefix AML.T followed by digits, for example AML.T0051 for LLM Prompt Injection, with sub-techniques for direct and indirect forms. The matrix is updated over time, so confirm IDs against the current release.

The tactics run roughly in the order of an attack. Reconnaissance gathers information such as public papers and model details; Resource Development prepares data, accounts or tools; Initial Access gets a foothold, for instance through ML supply chain compromise or a prompt delivered to an application; ML Model Access obtains query access or the model itself; Execution runs attacker-controlled behavior; Persistence, Privilege Escalation and Defense Evasion keep and extend control.

Later tactics include Discovery, Collection, ML Attack Staging (crafting adversarial data, poisoning, backdooring), Exfiltration (for example through the inference API) and Impact such as denial of service or integrity damage.

To map an incident, narrate it as a timeline and tag each step. A researcher reads a vendor's public documentation (Reconnaissance), obtains API access (ML Model Access), crafts inputs that bypass a filter (Defense Evasion with a technique such as evading the model), and abuses a connected tool to leak data (Exfiltration). Each tag links to a technique page with mitigations and real case studies.

Typical IDs worth recognizing include AML.T0020 poison training data, AML.T0018 backdoor ML model, AML.T0043 craft adversarial data, AML.T0024 exfiltration via ML inference API and AML.T0054 LLM jailbreak.

Use ATLAS in three ways. For threat modeling, walk the matrix and ask which techniques apply to your system. For detection, link each technique to telemetry you collect and to a detection rule. For reporting, cite technique IDs in findings and incident reports so that other teams can look up mitigations and compare with public cases. Pair ATLAS with ATT&CK, since most AI incidents also involve conventional techniques such as credential theft and cloud misconfiguration. Treat ATLAS as a vocabulary and checklist, not a guarantee of completeness.

snippet.label: Mapping notes (example)
snippet.text:
Step 1  recon: read public API docs            -> Reconnaissance
Step 2  obtain trial API key                  -> ML Model Access (AML.T0040)
Step 3  repeated queries to clone behavior    -> Exfiltration (AML.T0024)
Step 4  prompt override of system rules       -> AML.T0051 LLM Prompt Injection

lessons.example: An internal red team report states: 'we got the bot to leak customer addresses'. Rewritten with ATLAS, it reads: Initial Access via a crafted document in the knowledge base (AML.T0051.001, indirect prompt injection), Execution through the bot's search tool, and Exfiltration by rendering a link containing the data. The mapped technique pages suggest mitigations: input filtering, output filtering, tool restrictions and monitoring.

lessons.title: NIST adversarial ML taxonomy
lessons.why: NIST AI 100-2 classifies attacks by goal, capability and knowledge, which helps you choose defenses by class.

p: NIST AI 100-2, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, is a US government publication that organizes attacks into a consistent structure and defines the terms. The structure uses three axes: the attacker's goal or objective, the attacker's capabilities and the attacker's knowledge of the system. It is updated periodically, and recent editions add a separate treatment of generative AI. Using it gives auditors and vendors a common vocabulary.

For predictive AI the main classes are evasion, poisoning and privacy attacks. Evasion changes inputs at inference time so the model errs, as with adversarial examples. Poisoning corrupts training data or the model, and includes availability, targeted and backdoor variants. Privacy attacks extract information about training data or the model, such as membership inference, reconstruction and model extraction.

For generative AI the taxonomy adds abuse violations and prompt-injection-style attacks, including direct and indirect injection, where the model is made to produce harmful content or take unintended actions.

Attacker goals are described by the property violated: availability breakdown (the system stops working), integrity violation (wrong outputs, targeted or untargeted), privacy compromise (disclosure of data or model details) and, for generative AI, abuse. Capabilities describe what the attacker controls: training data, the model, testing data, labels, source code or only queries. Knowledge ranges from white-box (full access to architecture and weights) through gray-box (partial) to black-box (queries only).
These axes determine feasibility: a black-box attacker with only queries has fewer options than an insider with data access.

Classify each finding by class, goal and attacker knowledge. A finding such as 'repeated queries reconstruct the classifier's decision boundary' becomes a privacy attack, model extraction, black-box with query access. That classification guides controls: rate limiting and output minimization for extraction, data vetting for poisoning, adversarial training and input checks for evasion. Pairing NIST classes with ATLAS techniques and OWASP LLM risks in the same report gives each audience a framing it recognizes while keeping a single underlying finding.

snippet.label: Classification card
snippet.text:
finding : repeated queries clone classifier
class   : privacy attack (model extraction)
goal    : privacy compromise
knowledge: black-box, query access only
control : rate limits, output minimization, monitoring

lessons.example: Three summaries arrive. A: a sticker on a stop sign makes a vision model misread it. B: ten thousand mislabeled samples were added to a public dataset. C: an attacker asks a model to repeat random text and recovers a stranger's email address. Classified: A is evasion (integrity, test-time input control), B is poisoning (integrity, training data control), C is a privacy attack on training data memorization.

lessons.title: Attacker capabilities and risk rating
lessons.why: Rating threats by who can exploit them and how badly prevents wasted effort on unlikely attacks.

p: Attacker access is the biggest driver of feasibility. A white-box attacker has the weights and architecture, so can compute gradients and craft precise adversarial inputs; this is realistic after a model leak or for open-weight models. A gray-box attacker knows something, such as the model family, the training data source or the output scores. A black-box attacker only sends inputs and sees outputs, which is the typical position of an internet user, though research shows many white-box results transfer to black-box targets.
Also consider insider access to training data, the registry or logs, which bypasses many technical defenses.

Rate each threat on likelihood and impact. Likelihood depends on attacker access needed, skill, cost, how visible the attack is and whether public tools exist. Impact considers confidentiality, integrity, availability, safety, financial and legal consequences. A simple 1-5 scale for each and a product gives a score; qualitative High, Medium, Low also works if applied consistently. Document assumptions, because a threat that is low likelihood with query-only access may become high if the model weights are published.

Match mitigations to the scenario and layer them. For black-box abuse: authentication, rate limits, input and output filtering, monitoring and minimizing returned detail. For insider and supply chain threats: access control, separation of duties, signing, provenance and review. For integrity threats: adversarial testing, robust training and human review of high-impact decisions. For impact limiting: least-privilege tools and approval gates, because you can rarely guarantee the model is unmanipulable.
Accept, transfer or avoid residual risk explicitly, with an owner's sign-off.

Risk ratings decay. New public attack tools, a new model release or a new connector can change likelihood overnight. Tie the ranking to evidence: red team results, attack success rates, alert counts and incident history. Review the top items regularly and record why a score changed. Avoid two common errors: rating everything High, which hides priorities, and dismissing exotic-sounding attacks without checking whether the required access is actually available. A short written rationale next to each score makes the process auditable and easier to defend to stakeholders.

snippet.text:
ID  Threat                 Access    L  I  Score  Action
T1  Prompt injection->tool black-box  4  4  16     Scope tools, approval
T2  Weights leak           insider   2  5  10     Access control, DLP
T3  Query extraction       black-box 3  3   9     Rate limit, monitor
T4  Poisoned wiki page     gray-box  3  4  12     Source vetting

lessons.example: A fraud team scores two threats. Threat A: an external user crafts transactions that evade the fraud model, black-box, likelihood 4, impact 4, score 16. Threat B: a stolen checkpoint enables white-box attacks, requires insider or cloud compromise, likelihood 2, impact 5, score 10. They fund adversarial testing and rate limits first, and put bucket access hardening and checkpoint encryption on the next sprint.

labs.objective: Select the matching ATLAS tactics and technique IDs in order.

steps.do: Read the incident narrative.
Select tactic for reading public docs.
steps.see: Reconnaissance (AML.T0000 style: search open technical sources).

steps.do: Select tactic and technique for trial account queries.
steps.see: ML Model Access: AML.T0040 ML Model Inference API Access.

steps.do: Select staging step for copying the model.
steps.see: ML Attack Staging: create proxy ML model.

steps.do: Select the final step.
steps.see: Defense Evasion: AML.T0015 Evade ML Model with crafted data (AML.T0043).

labs.answer: Sequence: Reconnaissance, ML Model Access (AML.T0040), ML Attack Staging with a proxy model trained from query results, then Defense Evasion using crafted adversarial data (AML.T0043 / AML.T0015). Mitigations: rate limiting, query monitoring, limited output detail.

labs.title: Classify attacks by NIST taxonomy
labs.scenario: You receive ten fictional attack summaries from a vendor tracker and must classify each by NIST AI 100-2 class and attacker knowledge.
labs.objective: Sort ten attack summaries into evasion, poisoning, privacy or abuse and name attacker knowledge level.

steps.do: Item 1: crafted pixels make a classifier misread a sign (weights known).
Item 2: mislabeled samples added to a public dataset.
Item 3: queries reveal whether a record was in training.
Item 4: trigger phrase flips a sentiment model after fine-tuning.
Item 5: web page tells a chatbot to leak its chat history.
Item 6: query sequences clone a model.
Submit remaining items 7-10 classification.
steps.see: Score 10/10 after corrections; hint shown for item 8.

labs.answer: Evasion: 1 and similar test-time input tricks. Poisoning: 2 and 4. Privacy: 3 and 6. Abuse or injection: 5. Knowledge: white-box for item 1, black-box for query-only attacks, and training data or model control for poisoning.
labs.hint: Ask when in the life cycle the attacker acts and what they control.
